title: MARRIAGE IS HOLY—BUT SCRIPTURE NEVER SAYS EVERY CHRISTIAN MUST MARRY
paragraphs: MARRIAGE IS HOLY—BUT SCRIPTURE NEVER SAYS EVERY CHRISTIAN MUST MARRY
What If the Life You Keep Calling “Incomplete” Is the Very Life Christ Intends to Use for His Kingdom?
There is a particular kind of pain that rarely gets mentioned from the pulpit.
It happens when everyone else seems to be moving forward.
Another engagement.
Another wedding.
Another pregnancy announcement.
Another smiling photograph with a caption about “God’s perfect timing.”
And you are happy for them.
You really are.
But somewhere beneath the congratulations, beneath the heart emojis, beneath the smile you have learned to wear so well, a question whispers from somewhere you don't like admitting exists:
“What is wrong with me?”
Maybe you are 27.
Maybe 37.
Maybe 57.
Maybe you have never married.
Maybe you thought you would be married by now.
Maybe you were married once and buried the person you thought would grow old beside you.
Maybe betrayal destroyed what you believed would last forever.
Maybe divorce left scars you still don't know how to explain.
Maybe you desire marriage deeply, but the right person has never appeared.
Or maybe—and this can feel almost forbidden to say in some Christian circles—you genuinely do not believe God is calling you to marriage.
And somewhere along the way, Christian culture may have accidentally taught you something Scripture never did:
That marriage is graduation and singleness is the waiting room.
That the married Christian has “arrived,” while the unmarried Christian is still waiting for God to finish writing the story.
But what if Jesus never said that?
What if Paul never said that?
What if the Bible honors marriage magnificently without ever turning marriage into a requirement for every disciple?
And what if some of the shame you have been carrying was never placed on your shoulders by Jesus at all?
Read that again.
Because somebody has spent years asking God to remove a stigma that God never gave them.
Marriage is holy.
Marriage is beautiful.
Marriage was designed by God.
Marriage must not be mocked, cheapened, casually discarded, sexually corrupted, or treated as merely a social contract.
Scripture reaches all the way back to creation and declares:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” — Genesis 2:24
Jesus Himself reaches back to that creation account when teaching about marriage in Matthew 19:4–6.
Christianity is not anti-marriage.
Far from it.
Hebrews 13:4 says in Greek:
“Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος…”
Timios ho gamos en pasin kai hē koitē amiantos.
“Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled…”
The word τίμιος—timios—carries the sense of something precious, honored, valuable.
Marriage is not disposable.
It is not merely a ceremony, a tax status, a romantic accessory, or two people agreeing to stay together until happiness becomes inconvenient.
Biblically, marriage carries covenantal weight.
And yet here is where Christians must be careful.
Saying marriage is holy is not the same as saying marriage is mandatory.
Calling marriage good does not require calling singleness defective.
Honoring husbands and wives does not require treating unmarried believers as unfinished human beings.
Because when Jesus Christ walked this earth in perfect humanity, He never married.
Think about what that means.

If marriage were necessary for a human life to be spiritually complete, emotionally meaningful, or fully pleasing to God, we would be forced into an impossible conclusion about the sinless Son of God.
Jesus was not half a man because He had no wife.
He was not waiting for His “real life” to begin.
He was not incomplete.
He was not behind.
He was not less mature.
He was not less human.
His identity was not constructed around a wedding ring.
His life was completely surrendered to the Father.
And then Jesus said something astonishing.
While discussing marriage, divorce, and the disciples' reaction to His teaching, Christ acknowledged that not everyone would live the same marital story.
Matthew 19:12 preserves His words in Greek:
“εἰσὶν… εὐνοῦχοι… οἵτινες εὐνούχισαν ἑαυτοὺς διὰ τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν.”
There are those who have embraced such a life “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.”
Then Jesus says:
“ὁ δυνάμενος χωρεῖν χωρείτω.”
Ho dynamenos chōrein chōreitō.
In essence: the one able to receive this, let that person receive it.
Jesus did not command every disciple to remain unmarried.
But neither did He command every disciple to marry.
That matters.
Then Paul walks directly into the conversation.
And if anyone still believes every faithful Christian must eventually marry, 1 Corinthians 7 becomes extraordinarily difficult to explain away.
Paul writes:
“To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them if they remain as I am.” — 1 Corinthians 7:8
Notice the word.
Good.
Not shameful.
Not tragic.
Not second-class.
Not “good temporarily until God finally sends somebody.”
Good.

Paul then makes clear that marriage is also good and appropriate. He explicitly says that if people marry, they have not sinned. His concern in the chapter is not to manufacture a hierarchy of human worth but to teach believers how to live faithfully before Christ in the circumstances and callings in which they find themselves.
Later he explains one of the potential advantages of unmarried life:
“But I would have you without carefulness. He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord.” — 1 Corinthians 7:32
That does not mean married Christians cannot be passionately devoted to Jesus.
Christian history is filled with husbands and wives who have served Christ beautifully.
A godly marriage can preach the Gospel without a microphone.
A husband laying down selfishness to love his wife sacrificially can reflect Christ's covenant love.
A wife faithfully loving her husband can display extraordinary grace.
A Christian home can become a refuge.
Children can be discipled.
Strangers can be welcomed.
Meals can become ministry.
Hospitality can become worship.
Forgiveness inside marriage can become a living testimony that Jesus still resurrects things human beings thought were dead.
Marriage can be breathtakingly holy.
But singleness can be holy too.
That is the truth we sometimes seem afraid to say.
The unmarried believer is not a Christian in the lobby waiting to be admitted into adulthood.
She can disciple.
He can preach.
She can evangelize.
He can serve.
She can travel where God sends her.
He can pour himself into ministry.
She can nurture spiritual sons and daughters.
He can become a faithful uncle, brother, mentor, missionary, pastor, servant, friend, giver, teacher, intercessor, caregiver, or witness.
The Kingdom of God does not inspect your left hand before deciding whether your life can matter.
And perhaps someone needs that sentence tonight.
Because you have been measuring your worth with somebody else's wedding photographs.
Stop.
Not because marriage doesn't matter.
Because Christ matters more.
Marriage is a gift.
It is not a god.
And when a good gift becomes the condition upon which you permit yourself to believe your life is meaningful, that gift has quietly begun occupying a throne it was never meant to have.
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Some people do not merely desire marriage.
They believe marriage will save them.
“If I can just find somebody, I won't feel lonely anymore.”
“If somebody finally chooses me, I'll know I'm valuable.”
“If I get married, I'll stop struggling sexually.”
“If I get married, I'll finally be happy.”
“If I get married, then my life can begin.”
But marriage cannot bear the weight of being your messiah.
Your husband cannot save your soul.
Your wife cannot heal every wound.
Romance cannot cleanse guilt.
Sex cannot provide eternal identity.
A wedding cannot reconcile you to God.
Only Jesus can do that.
And some married people know this more painfully than anybody.
You can sleep beside someone and still feel lonely.
You can wear a ring and still battle insecurity.
You can have beautiful wedding photographs and a bleeding marriage.
You can sit beside your spouse in church while privately wondering how two people living under one roof became strangers.
Marriage is holy.
Marriage is also inhabited by sinners.
That means marriage needs the Gospel just as desperately as singleness does.
The single person needs Jesus.
The married person needs Jesus.
The divorced person needs Jesus.
The widow needs Jesus.
The person desperate to marry needs Jesus.
The person called to remain single needs Jesus.
The person whose marriage is thriving needs Jesus.
The person whose marriage is hanging by a thread needs Jesus.
The ultimate dividing line in eternity will never be married versus unmarried.
It will be whether you belong to Christ.
That is why your deepest question cannot merely be:
“Will I ever get married?”
There is a more important question.
“Does Jesus have all of me?”
Because you can find a spouse and lose yourself spiritually.
You can obtain the relationship you prayed for while gradually abandoning the God you once prayed to.
You can become so obsessed with finding “the one” that you forget there is already One before whom every knee will bow.
Jesus Christ is not the consolation prize for people who could not find a spouse.
He is the treasure.
He is the Bridegroom of His redeemed people.
He is the crucified and risen Lord.
He is the Lamb who was slain.
He is the King who is coming again.
Your relationship status does not determine your access to Him.
And maybe this is where the tears come.
Because perhaps nobody ever told you that you were allowed to stop apologizing for being unmarried.
Maybe family gatherings have become interrogations.
“When are you getting married?”
“Why are you still single?”
“You're too picky.”
“Your biological clock is ticking.”
“Don't worry, God has someone for you.”
Maybe they mean well.
But notice what that final sentence assumes.
Does Scripture promise every Christian a spouse?
No.
God may indeed lead you into marriage.
Pray about it.
Desire it without shame.
Prepare yourself for covenant rather than fantasy.
Seek wisdom.
Develop character.
Refuse desperation.
Do not lower biblical convictions simply because loneliness has become loud.
But never turn a personal desire into a divine promise God never made.
God promised something infinitely greater than universal marriage.
He promised Himself.
“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.” — Hebrews 13:5
That promise belongs to the believer whether there is another person sleeping beside you or not.
And if God does lead you into marriage, enter it knowing your spouse is not your Savior.
If God calls you to a season of singleness, do not waste that season treating it as meaningless.
If He grants you lifelong singleness for concentrated Kingdom service, do not allow people to make you ashamed of an offering Christ Himself dignified.
And if you desperately want marriage while God has not yet provided it, you do not have to pretend the waiting doesn't hurt.
Christian maturity is not pretending.
You can tell Jesus you are lonely.
You can cry.
You can grieve dreams that haven't happened.
You can admit that another wedding invitation sometimes hurts.
You can rejoice with someone and then go home and weep.
Faith is not emotional anesthesia.
Jesus is not frightened by your honesty.
Bring Him the ache.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the fear.
Bring Him the sexual temptation.
Bring Him the disappointment.
Bring Him the nights when you wonder whether anybody will ever choose you.
Then remember the cross.
Before you were impressive enough.
Before you fixed yourself.
Before you had anything worthy to offer Him.
Christ moved toward sinners.
The Gospel does not say, “Become desirable enough and perhaps God will choose you.”
The Gospel announces that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
He carried sin.
He bore judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
Your greatest scandal was never that you were single.
Your greatest scandal was sin.
And your greatest need was never a wedding.
It was redemption.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
This is where Jesus rewrites everything.
The world tells you your worth depends upon being wanted by another human being.
Jesus points toward a bloodstained cross and shows you what your redemption cost.
Culture asks whether somebody put a ring on your finger.
The Gospel asks whether Christ has made your heart new.
Culture says, “Find someone who completes you.”
Jesus says, in effect, “Come to Me.”
And when Christ becomes the center, something beautiful happens.
Marriage can stop being an idol and become a gift.
Singleness can stop being a verdict and become a place of faithfulness.
Widowhood does not become easy, but it does not become meaningless.
Divorce does not have to become your permanent identity.
Past sexual sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Failure does not have to have the last word.
Shame does not get authorship rights over a life purchased by Jesus.
Maybe your story contains things you wish you could erase.
Maybe you compromised because you were terrified of being alone.
Maybe you stayed with someone you knew was pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe you crossed sexual boundaries and have been carrying secret shame ever since.
Maybe you broke somebody's heart.
Maybe somebody broke yours.
Maybe you have lived with pornography, lust, emotional dependency, adultery, bitterness, or regret.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Grace does not call sin harmless.
Grace calls sinners home.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the mercy of God turning you away from what is killing you and toward the One who gives life.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the scandal never happened.
He rewrites everything by bringing sinners through repentance into forgiveness, cleansing, restoration, obedience, and a new life centered upon Him.
So whether you are married or single, stop asking your relationship status to tell you who you are.
Ask Christ.
If you belong to Jesus, your first identity is not single.
Not married.
Not divorced.
Not widowed.
Not rejected.
Not unwanted.
Not somebody's ex.
Not somebody's future spouse.
You are Christ's.
And that changes the question.
Instead of only asking, “God, when will You send me somebody?”
Perhaps tonight you need to ask:
“Jesus, what do You want to do with the life I already have?”
That question can change everything.
There are prayers you can pray now.
People you can disciple now.
Neighbors you can love now.
Scripture you can study now.
Habits you can surrender now.
People you can forgive now.
Ministry you can support now.
The Gospel you can share now.
Holiness you can pursue now.
You do not need a wedding certificate before obedience becomes possible.
Your calling to follow Jesus has already begun.

And if this exposed something hidden in you—an idol, a fear, shame over being single, resentment toward God, desperation for marriage, or the belief that another human being must complete what only Christ can redeem—don't hide behind another religious smile.
Be honest.
Someone reading beneath this article may desperately need proof that God is still faithful when life does not follow the timeline we imagined.
Then think of one person who needs this truth.
Not fifty.
One.
The unmarried friend who laughs at the jokes but cries afterward.
The Christian woman wondering whether she is somehow less valuable because nobody has proposed.
The man who is considering marrying someone who pulls him away from Jesus simply because he is tired of being alone.
The divorced believer convinced his usefulness to God ended with his marriage.
The widow who feels invisible.
The married couple who needs to remember that their spouse was never meant to replace Christ.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too. Sometimes one Gospel-centered article arrives in a person's life at precisely the moment their heart has become willing to listen.
It doesn't.
Only Jesus saves.
Not because God needs your money.
He doesn't.

But because Gospel ministry in this world requires believers who do more than consume what strengthens them. Scripture repeatedly celebrates willing, generous partnership in Gospel work. If this ministry is bearing biblical fruit in your life, supporting it is one practical way you can help Gospel-centered teaching keep reaching people who are hurting, searching, doubting, repenting, rebuilding, and discovering Jesus.
Pray.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Encourage someone.

Because glorifying God is bigger than supporting any single ministry. We glorify Him by trusting Christ, obeying His Word, loving people, proclaiming His Gospel, serving faithfully, giving freely rather than under compulsion, and using whatever He has placed in our hands for His Kingdom.
Married?
Make your marriage about Jesus.
Single?
Make your singleness about Jesus.
Waiting?
Wait with Jesus.
Heartbroken?
Run toward Jesus.
Widowed?
Hold onto Jesus.
Divorced and repentant over your own failures?
Come to Jesus.
Ashamed of your past?
Come to Jesus.
Afraid nobody will ever choose you?
Look again at the cross.
Because your life does not become valuable when somebody finally says, “I do.”
Your life finds its deepest meaning when you can look at the crucified and risen Christ and say:
“I am Yours.”
And perhaps the chapter you thought God forgot to finish is not unfinished at all.
Perhaps Jesus is already writing something you could not recognize because you were waiting for the story to look like everybody else's.
Marriage is holy.
But marriage is not your Savior.
Singleness may be difficult.
But singleness is not your shame.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And whether He leads you toward a wedding altar or gives you grace to walk a different road, the highest calling of your life remains exactly the same:
Follow Him.
Because one day, when every earthly title disappears and every human story reaches its final page, the question will not be whether you managed to become somebody's husband or wife.
The question that echoes into eternity is whether you belonged to Jesus.
So don't spend your entire life waiting for another human being to begin a story Christ has already called you to live.
